scr_ap_accounts_payable_charts.purpose: Opens the A/P charting area where payables data is rendered graphically — vendor aging bands and invoice-volume trends — for the property-level review deck and the owner's monthly operating package, filtered by period, book and location.
scr_ap_accounts_payable_charts.outcome: Payables exposure is visible as a shape rather than a number, so an aging tail or a spend spike is caught before the owner asks about it.
scr_ap_accounts_payable_charts.rootCause: Owners and asset managers read pictures faster than a 40-page aging. A chart is the first place a 90-day tail on a single roofing vendor or a month with double the usual invoice count becomes obvious. The risk is that the chart is drawn from a different filter set than the aging it is supposed to summarize, so the picture and the 2010 Accounts Payable control balance tell different stories in the same package.
scr_ap_accounts_payable_charts.ifSkipped: Aging concentration and spend anomalies stay buried in tabular reports until an owner or auditor finds them first.
gaap: COSO 2013 — information and communication (reporting to those charged with governance)
ASC 235 — consistency of presentation between periods
redFlags: Chart period or book differs from the aging report it accompanies
Charts run on posted-only data while unposted accruals sit in the batch
On-hold invoices silently excluded from the chart but included in the aging
scr_ap_accounts_payable_charts.yardi: Yardi Voyager: Analytics > Payable Analytics dashboards and YBI/Orion payables charts; standard graphs off the Payable Aging and Payable Register.

scr_ap_list_of_a_p_charts.purpose: Enumerates the two payables charts RealPage ships — the vendor aging chart and the A/P invoice analysis chart — so the accountant picks the one that answers the question being asked rather than building an ad hoc pivot in Excel.
scr_ap_list_of_a_p_charts.outcome: The reviewer knows which of the two standard charts to run, and every property in the portfolio uses the same two, so cross-property comparison is valid.
scr_ap_list_of_a_p_charts.rootCause: When each property accountant invents their own payables graphic, the owner receives 40 differently-scaled pictures and cannot compare them. Standardizing on the shipped chart set is what makes a portfolio roll-up meaningful, and it is also what keeps the definitions — which invoices count as aged, which as disputed — identical across entities.
scr_ap_list_of_a_p_charts.ifSkipped: Each property produces its own payables visual with its own definition of aging, and the portfolio roll-up compares incomparable numbers.
gaap: ASC 235-10-50 — consistent application of accounting presentation
COSO 2013 — quality of information used in monitoring
redFlags: Properties substituting hand-built Excel graphics for the standard charts
Aging bucket definitions differing between the chart and the aging report

scr_ap_examples_of_chart_types.purpose: Shows which visual forms — column, line, pie, stacked bar — are actually available for a given payables data set, because chart type is not free choice: aging buckets need a stacked or grouped column, spend trend needs a line, vendor concentration needs a ranked bar.
scr_ap_examples_of_chart_types.outcome: The chart form matches the question, so the reviewer reads concentration and trend correctly instead of being misled by the wrong encoding.
scr_ap_examples_of_chart_types.rootCause: A pie chart of vendor spend across 200 vendors communicates nothing; a line chart of aging buckets implies a continuity that does not exist. Picking a form the data does not support is how a reviewer concludes that payables are flat when in fact one vendor moved from 30 days to 90. The available-type restriction exists because RealPage will not render a form the underlying data set cannot support.
scr_ap_examples_of_chart_types.ifSkipped: A poorly chosen chart form hides vendor concentration or an aging shift that the same numbers would have made obvious in a table.
gaap: COSO 2013 — relevant, quality information for decision-making
redFlags: Pie charts used for long-tail vendor spend
Truncated or non-zero-based value axes exaggerating a spend trend
Chart type changed between months so the owner cannot compare

scr_ap_working_with_charts.purpose: Covers what happens to a payables chart after it is built — customizing, storing, emailing, memorizing its parameters, scheduling it, and pinning it to a dashboard — so a recurring owner deliverable runs the same way every month without being rebuilt.
scr_ap_working_with_charts.outcome: A memorized, scheduled chart reproduces identical filters each period, and dashboard tiles stay tied to the report they summarize.
scr_ap_working_with_charts.rootCause: Memorized parameters are a control, not a convenience. A chart rebuilt by hand each month drifts — someone adds a property, drops a book, or changes the as-of date — and the owner sees a payables trend that reflects the filter change, not the business. Scheduled distribution also pushes vendor-level data outside the platform, which puts the delivery inside the SOC 1 boundary the owner's auditor tests.
scr_ap_working_with_charts.ifSkipped: Manually rebuilt charts drift period to period, and a trend line shows a filter change rather than a real movement in payables.
gaap: COSO 2013 — control activities over reporting (completeness and accuracy of information produced by the entity)
SOC 1 — controls over report distribution and data leaving the system
redFlags: Scheduled charts still emailing a terminated employee or a former owner contact
Memorized parameters carrying a hard-coded as-of date instead of a relative period
Dashboard tile refreshing on a different book than the statement beside it
scr_ap_working_with_charts.yardi: Yardi Voyager: Report Scheduler / Task Runner for recurring distribution, memorized report filters, and Voyager dashboard widgets.

scr_ap_about_the_accounts_payable_applic.purpose: Orients the user to the full RealPage payables application — vendor creation and merge, invoice entry and posting, advances and adjustments, payment approval, and checking-account reconciliation — and notes that the Company application controls subscription and the Setup tab controls configuration.
scr_ap_about_the_accounts_payable_applic.outcome: Staff understand the module boundary: what posts to 2010 Accounts Payable here versus what belongs in Cash Management or the GL.
scr_ap_about_the_accounts_payable_applic.rootCause: New offshore staff routinely enter transactions in the wrong module — a wire recorded as a journal entry instead of a manual payment, or a vendor credit booked as a GL adjustment — which breaks the subledger-to-control-account tie-out at month end. Knowing which objects live in payables is the prerequisite for the 2010 reconciliation ever agreeing.
scr_ap_about_the_accounts_payable_applic.ifSkipped: Transactions land in the wrong module and the A/P subledger no longer ties to the 2010 Accounts Payable control account.
gaap: COSO 2013 — control environment and defined responsibilities
ASC 405 — liabilities recognition and derecognition
redFlags: Payables activity entered as manual journal entries, bypassing the subledger
Modules subscribed without the corresponding approval configuration enabled
scr_ap_about_the_accounts_payable_applic.yardi: Yardi Voyager: the Payables module (Payables > Vendor, Payable Entry, Check Processing) plus PAYscan for invoice capture and workflow.

scr_ap_add_a_vendor.purpose: Creates the vendor master record — legal name, remit-to address, TIN and 1099 eligibility, payment terms, insurance certificates and ACH banking detail — before any invoice can be coded or paid to that party.
scr_ap_add_a_vendor.outcome: A complete, verified payee exists with the tax and banking attributes that drive year-end reporting and payment routing.
scr_ap_add_a_vendor.rootCause: The vendor master is the single highest-value fraud target in property accounting: whoever can add a payee with banking detail can move cash. It is also where 1099 exposure is created or avoided, because the TIN and 1099 flag captured at setup are what year-end reporting accumulates against. Adding a vendor from an emailed request, without an independently sourced W-9 and a call-back to a known number, is the precise failure pattern behind business-email-compromise losses at managed properties.
scr_ap_add_a_vendor.ifSkipped: Invoices cannot be processed, or worse, a fictitious or hijacked payee is created and paid before anyone reconciles the vendor master.
gaap: IRC §6041 — information reporting and TIN collection via Form W-9
IRC §3406 — backup withholding on a missing or incorrect TIN
COSO 2013 — segregation of duties over master data and disbursement
NACHA Operating Rules — validation of receiver banking detail
redFlags: Vendor added by the same person who can release payments
Remit-to address matching an employee address or a mail drop
No W-9 on file for a vendor set up as 1099 eligible
Banking detail taken from an emailed PDF without call-back verification
scr_ap_add_a_vendor.yardi: Yardi Voyager: Payables > Vendor (Add) with the 1099, EFT and insurance tabs; VendorCafe for vendor-supplied onboarding and compliance documents.

scr_ap_edit_a_vendor.purpose: Amends an existing vendor record — a new remit-to address, changed terms, renewed insurance, a corrected TIN, or revised ACH banking instructions — on a payee that already has posted history and open invoices.
scr_ap_edit_a_vendor.outcome: The vendor's current attributes are accurate for the next payment run without disturbing the history behind already-posted invoices.
scr_ap_edit_a_vendor.rootCause: Editing an existing vendor is more dangerous than creating one, because the payee already looks legitimate to every downstream reviewer. A changed bank account on a long-standing landscaping vendor draws no attention in the payment proposal, yet it redirects every future ACH. Changing the 1099 name or TIN mid-year also splits the year's payments across two tax identities unless the change is dated and understood.
scr_ap_edit_a_vendor.ifSkipped: Payments go to a stale address or a closed bank account, insurance lapses go unnoticed, and 1099s are issued to the wrong taxpayer.
gaap: COSO 2013 — authorization and independent verification of master-data changes
NACHA Operating Rules — change of receiver account detail
IRC §6041 — accuracy of payee name and TIN on information returns
redFlags: Bank-detail change followed within days by an unusually large payment
Vendor edits made outside business hours or by a single unreviewed user
Insurance expiry dates extended in the system without a new certificate attached
scr_ap_edit_a_vendor.yardi: Yardi Voyager: Payables > Vendor (Edit) with change history under the record's Audit/History function.

scr_ap_add_an_a_p_invoice.purpose: Enters a vendor invoice into payables — vendor, invoice number and date, service period, property, GL coding by line, and any job or cost-code allocation — creating the liability that the owner's operating statement and cash forecast both depend on.
scr_ap_add_an_a_p_invoice.outcome: A coded, dated liability enters the approval workflow and, on posting, credits 2010 Accounts Payable with the expense charged to the right property and period.
scr_ap_add_an_a_p_invoice.rootCause: Invoice entry is where the owner's income statement is actually written. Three decisions made on this screen decide the financials: which property bears the cost, which period the service belongs to (the accrual cut-off), and whether the spend is an expense or a capital addition. A turn invoice coded to 6110 Repairs & Maintenance when the work was a full unit renovation understates capitalized basis and overstates operating expense, which flows straight into the NOI the owner is valued on.
scr_ap_add_an_a_p_invoice.ifSkipped: Liabilities go unrecorded, the period's expenses are understated, and the accrual the accountant books at close has to be guessed rather than sourced.
gaap: ASC 720 / accrual basis — expense recognized in the period the service was rendered
ASC 360-10-30 — capitalization versus repair and maintenance
ASC 340-10 — prepaid assets for services spanning periods
COSO 2013 — completeness and accuracy of transaction recording
redFlags: Duplicate invoice number for the same vendor
Service period crossing the cut-off but dated in the later period
Capital work coded to 6110 Repairs & Maintenance to stay inside the operating budget
Invoice property differing from the property named on the vendor's invoice
scr_ap_add_an_a_p_invoice.yardi: Yardi Voyager: Payables > Payable Entry (single) or Payable Batch; OCR-captured invoices via PAYscan > Invoice Register.

scr_ap_edit_an_a_p_invoice.purpose: Corrects an invoice already in the system — amount, dates, coding or description — noting that invoices transferred from OneSite Leasing & Rents can only be changed at the Top level, and that a saved change in an open period re-posts the GL lines.
scr_ap_edit_an_a_p_invoice.outcome: The corrected invoice carries the right amount and coding, and its GL lines are re-posted to match without a separate adjusting entry.
scr_ap_edit_an_a_p_invoice.rootCause: Editing is the quiet path around approval. An invoice approved at $4,800 and then edited to $9,600 in an open period re-posts at the higher amount, and whether it re-enters the approval workflow depends entirely on configuration. Auditors test exactly this: they pull approved invoices, compare the approved amount to the posted amount, and ask why they differ. The OneSite top-level restriction exists because the source system owns the property-level detail.
scr_ap_edit_an_a_p_invoice.ifSkipped: Known-wrong amounts and coding stay in the ledger, and the correction turns into a reversal-and-re-entry that clutters the vendor history.
gaap: ASC 250-10 — correction of an error in the period identified
COSO 2013 — changes to authorized transactions require re-authorization
redFlags: Post-approval amount increases that did not re-trigger the approval workflow
Edits to invoices already selected in an open payment request
Attempts to edit a closed-period invoice instead of reversing it

scr_ap_delete_an_a_p_invoice.purpose: Removes an invoice outright, available only while the Enable reversal of unpaid A/P Invoices configuration is cleared — otherwise the system offers Reverse instead, and OneSite-transferred invoices can only be deleted at the Top Level.
scr_ap_delete_an_a_p_invoice.outcome: A genuinely erroneous or duplicated entry leaves the system, or, where reversal is enabled, is reversed with the audit trail preserved.
scr_ap_delete_an_a_p_invoice.rootCause: Deletion destroys evidence. When a posted invoice is deleted in an open period its GL lines vanish, which means the A/P register no longer explains the movement in 2010 Accounts Payable and an auditor tracing a gap in invoice numbers finds nothing. That is why mature owners disable delete and force reversal — a reversal leaves both the original and the offsetting entry visible. Deletion should be reserved for drafts that never posted.
scr_ap_delete_an_a_p_invoice.ifSkipped: Duplicate or test entries inflate the aging, get selected in a payment run, and the vendor is paid twice.
gaap: COSO 2013 — audit trail retention and evidence of control operation
SOC 1 — completeness of the transaction record for the service auditor
redFlags: Posted invoices deleted rather than reversed
Delete enabled in an environment subject to a SOC 1 examination
Gaps in the invoice sequence with no reversal record

scr_ap_reclassify_an_a_p_invoice.purpose: Changes the GL coding of a posted invoice that is not in a closed period, moving the debit between expense accounts or properties while leaving the 2010 Accounts Payable credit and the vendor balance untouched.
scr_ap_reclassify_an_a_p_invoice.outcome: The expense lands in the correct account and property without creating a second invoice or disturbing the payment status.
scr_ap_reclassify_an_a_p_invoice.rootCause: Coding errors surface after posting, usually during budget-variance review when a property manager asks why landscaping doubled. Reclassifying is the right remedy because deleting and re-entering changes the invoice's identity, breaks the payment link, and can re-trigger a duplicate-payment risk. The constraint that matters is period: once A/P is closed, reclassification is no longer available and the fix becomes a journal entry the accountant has to tie back manually.
scr_ap_reclassify_an_a_p_invoice.ifSkipped: Miscoded costs persist in the operating statement, variance explanations are fabricated to match, and the capital-versus-expense split reported to the owner is wrong.
gaap: ASC 250-10-45 — correction of classification errors
ASC 360-10-30 — capital versus expense reclassification
COSO 2013 — review controls over account coding
redFlags: Reclasses made after the owner package shipped without reissuing the statement
Repeated reclasses out of a budget line that is over, into one that is under
Reclassification from expense to capital late in the year with no supporting scope documentation

scr_ap_add_an_adjustment_credit_debit_me.purpose: Records a vendor credit or debit memo against the payables balance — a debit memo decreasing the amount due, a credit adjustment increasing the invoice — typically after a vendor statement reconciliation surfaces an overbilling, a return or a rebate.
scr_ap_add_an_adjustment_credit_debit_me.outcome: The vendor's open balance reflects the negotiated amount, and the credit is positioned to be applied in the next payment run rather than forgotten.
scr_ap_add_an_adjustment_credit_debit_me.rootCause: Vendor credits are routinely earned and never taken. A credit sitting unapplied on the vendor account does two things at once: it overstates 2010 Accounts Payable on the balance sheet and it lets the full invoice be paid in the next check run, turning the credit into a receivable the property will chase for months. Month-end vendor statement reconciliation is where these are found, and the memo is how they enter the ledger.
scr_ap_add_an_adjustment_credit_debit_me.ifSkipped: Earned credits are never taken, the property pays gross, and the payable balance carries amounts that are not actually owed.
gaap: ASC 405-20 — derecognition of a liability that is no longer owed
ASC 705-20 — consideration received from a vendor
COSO 2013 — reconciliation of subledger to vendor statements
redFlags: Credits left unapplied across multiple payment cycles
Debit memos raised without written vendor agreement
Credit memos used to force a disputed balance to zero rather than resolving the dispute

scr_ap_pay_a_p_invoices.purpose: Drives the payment run — filter to the invoices due, choose payment method, currency, request method and bank, apply open credits, and either stage the batch to the Outbox as a draft or release it with Pay Now; Pay by Entity switches to the entity-level view.
scr_ap_pay_a_p_invoices.outcome: A funded, approved batch of payments is staged or released against the correct bank account, with credits netted before cash leaves.
scr_ap_pay_a_p_invoices.rootCause: This is the screen where cash actually leaves the property, and three things must be true simultaneously: the invoices are approved, the bank has available cash after the owner distribution and debt service, and the vendor is not on hold. Releasing with Pay Now instead of staging to the Outbox collapses the maker-checker split that most management agreements require. Paying from the wrong bank on a multi-entity run creates Due To/Due From balances nobody reconciles until year end.
scr_ap_pay_a_p_invoices.ifSkipped: Vendors go unpaid past terms, late fees and service interruptions follow, and earned discounts lapse.
gaap: COSO 2013 — segregation of duties between invoice approval and payment release
NACHA Operating Rules — ACH origination authorization
ASC 850 — related-party transactions when paying across entities
redFlags: Pay Now used where policy requires Outbox staging and a second release
Payment run exceeding available cash after reserves and debt service
Cross-entity payments creating Due To/Due From balances with no settlement plan
Credits not applied before payment, so the vendor is paid gross
scr_ap_pay_a_p_invoices.yardi: Yardi Voyager: Payables > Check Processing (Create Checks / Auto Pay with bank and property filters), with EFT file generation for ACH.

scr_ap_select_a_p_invoices_to_pay.purpose: The selection grid inside the payment run where the accountant filters, picks individual invoices, types a partial amount in the Amount to pay column, and applies vendor credits before committing the batch.
scr_ap_select_a_p_invoices_to_pay.outcome: Only intended invoices, at the intended amounts, carry into the payment request, with partial payments recorded deliberately rather than by rounding.
scr_ap_select_a_p_invoices_to_pay.rootCause: Selection is where discretion enters the disbursement cycle, and discretion is what reviewers must be able to see. A saved filter that quietly omits on-hold invoices, or one still scoped to last week's due date, produces a batch that looks complete to an approver who never sees what was excluded. Partial payments typed into the Amount to pay column also need a reason — a disputed line, a retainage hold — or the residual balance ages with no explanation attached.
scr_ap_select_a_p_invoices_to_pay.ifSkipped: Batches are assembled from a stale filter, due invoices are missed while held ones slip through, and partial payments leave unexplained residuals in the aging.
gaap: COSO 2013 — completeness of the population presented for approval
Management agreement delegation-of-authority limits
redFlags: Saved filters excluding on-hold or disputed invoices without the approver knowing
Partial payments entered with no note explaining the withheld amount
Invoices selected before the final approval level completed

scr_ap_adding_a_manual_payment_2.purpose: Records a bill and its payment in a single step for disbursements that happened outside the check run — a wire to the tax collector, an auto-debited utility, an emergency hand check to a plumber at a flooded building.
scr_ap_adding_a_manual_payment_2.outcome: The off-cycle disbursement is on the ledger with its true bank date, so the bank reconciliation matches and the invoice cannot be paid a second time.
scr_ap_adding_a_manual_payment_2.rootCause: Off-cycle payments are recorded late almost by definition — the money moved first, the paperwork followed. Every day the entry is missing, the cash balance used for the next payment run is overstated and the same invoice remains selectable. Utility auto-debits and monthly loan payments are the worst offenders because they recur silently and nobody owns the entry until the bank rec finds an unexplained withdrawal.
scr_ap_adding_a_manual_payment_2.ifSkipped: The invoice is paid a second time in the next check run and the bank reconciliation carries an unidentified withdrawal for weeks.
gaap: COSO 2013 — controls over non-routine disbursements
UCC Article 4A — funds transfers
ASC 405-20 — liability settlement
redFlags: Manual payments entered days or weeks after the bank debit
Wires released without an approved invoice behind them
Recurring auto-debits with no standing entry owner
scr_ap_adding_a_manual_payment_2.yardi: Yardi Voyager: Payables > Manual Check to record a hand-written check or wire against open payables.

scr_ap_remove_an_a_p_invoice_from_the_pa.purpose: Pulls an invoice back out of a staged payment request — cancelling the whole request, or clearing a single line item's check box and saving — before the checks print or the ACH file transmits.
scr_ap_remove_an_a_p_invoice_from_the_pa.outcome: The disputed, duplicate or unfunded invoice drops out of the batch and returns to open status, and the remaining payments proceed on schedule.
scr_ap_remove_an_a_p_invoice_from_the_pa.rootCause: Something almost always changes between staging a batch and releasing it: a property manager reports the work was never completed, a duplicate surfaces, or treasury cuts the funding. Pulling one line is far safer than cancelling and rebuilding the whole request, because a rebuild re-exposes every other invoice to selection error. The timing constraint is absolute — once the ACH file is transmitted or the checks print, removal is no longer a removal, it is a void and a stop payment.
scr_ap_remove_an_a_p_invoice_from_the_pa.ifSkipped: A disputed or duplicate invoice is paid because nobody could stop it cleanly, and recovery becomes a vendor refund request.
gaap: COSO 2013 — ability to interrupt a transaction before it becomes irrevocable
NACHA Operating Rules — ACH entries cannot be unilaterally recalled after transmission
redFlags: Removal attempted after the ACH file was already transmitted
Whole requests cancelled and rebuilt when a single line removal would do
Removed invoices never revisited, so they age quietly

scr_ap_quick_check_entry_2.purpose: Records a check that was already written by hand outside the system — select the bank account it was drawn on, continue, enter the invoice detail, and post — bringing a physical check on-site into the ledger.
scr_ap_quick_check_entry_2.outcome: The hand-written check exists in the system with its real check number, so the check sequence is complete and the bank reconciliation can match it.
scr_ap_quick_check_entry_2.rootCause: On-site staff write emergency checks from the property checkbook when a vendor will not work otherwise. Those checks clear the bank whether or not accounting knows about them. Until the quick entry is made, the check number is a gap in the sequence, the bank reconciliation carries an unexplained clearing item, and the check is invisible to positive pay — which means the bank may reject it on presentation. Check stock in a leasing office is a negotiable instrument control issue, not an administrative one.
scr_ap_quick_check_entry_2.ifSkipped: Hand-written checks clear the bank as unidentified items, break the check-number sequence, and can be rejected by positive pay.
gaap: COSO 2013 — physical control over negotiable instruments and sequence accountability
UCC Article 3 — negotiable instruments
redFlags: Gaps in the on-site check sequence with no quick entry or void recorded
Hand-written checks over the on-site authority limit
Quick entries posted weeks after the check cleared
scr_ap_quick_check_entry_2.yardi: Yardi Voyager: Payables > Manual Check entry against the property bank, with check number recorded for the bank reconciliation.

scr_ap_download_a_csv_check_file.purpose: Exports selected checks as a CSV at check level with a chosen layout, used mainly when check printing is performed offsite by a print vendor or a shared services location, then confirms the checks to clear them from the print queue.
scr_ap_download_a_csv_check_file.outcome: A print vendor receives the payment file in the agreed layout and the checks leave the pending queue only once confirmed as handed off.
scr_ap_download_a_csv_check_file.rootCause: Outsourced check printing moves payee names, addresses, amounts and bank account data into a file that travels outside the platform, which puts the transfer squarely inside the SOC 1 boundary the owner's auditor examines. The operational risk is the Confirm step: confirm before the print vendor actually produces the checks and the batch disappears from the queue with nothing printed; skip Confirm and the same batch is downloaded twice and printed twice.
scr_ap_download_a_csv_check_file.ifSkipped: Offsite printing stalls, or the same check batch is exported repeatedly and duplicate checks are produced from the same payments.
gaap: SOC 1 — controls over data transmitted to a subservice organization
COSO 2013 — control over check stock and payment data handoff
NACHA / bank positive pay file transmission requirements
redFlags: CSV files with payee banking data stored on unsecured shared drives
Checks confirmed before the print vendor produced them
The same batch exported twice with no reconciliation of check numbers issued

scr_ap_print_checks.purpose: Produces the physical checks — select the checks to cut, choose stub detail for the check and the vendor copy, void any that need voiding first, print the PDF to a MICR-toner printer, then confirm the printed checks off the queue.
scr_ap_print_checks.outcome: Negotiable instruments are produced on controlled stock with correct MICR encoding, and the queue reflects exactly what was printed.
scr_ap_print_checks.rootCause: Check printing is the handling of negotiable instruments, so the controls are physical as much as systemic: check stock accounted for by number, MICR toner and alignment verified on a test print before the run, the signature plate or digital signature threshold enforced, and every misprinted form voided and retained rather than binned. The positive pay issue file must reach the bank the same day the checks print, because a check presented before the bank has the issue record is rejected and the vendor calls the property manager, not accounting.
scr_ap_print_checks.ifSkipped: Vendors are not paid, or checks print on misaligned or unaccounted stock and the bank rejects them at presentation.
gaap: UCC Article 3 and Article 4 — negotiable instruments and bank deposits
COSO 2013 — physical safeguards over assets and sequence accountability
SOC 1 — disbursement controls tested by the owner's service auditor
redFlags: Positive pay file not transmitted the same day checks print
Misprinted check stock discarded instead of voided and retained by number
Checks above the signature-plate threshold released without a manual second signature
Blank check stock stored unlocked in the leasing office
scr_ap_print_checks.yardi: Yardi Voyager: Payables > Check Processing > Print Checks with the bank's check layout and MICR settings from Setup > Bank.

scr_ap_void_a_check.purpose: Voids a check that was issued in error, lost, stale-dated or never received — found on the check register, voided with a void date and a memo — reversing DR 2010 Accounts Payable / CR 1110 Operating Cash so the invoice returns to open for reissue.
scr_ap_void_a_check.outcome: Cash and the payable are restored, the check is removed from the bank reconciliation's outstanding list, and the invoice can be reissued cleanly.
scr_ap_void_a_check.rootCause: The void date is the decision that gets this wrong. Voiding into the original period after the owner statement was issued restates a month that has already been reported; voiding into the current open period keeps the history intact and is what controllers require. The other failure is voiding a check that has already cleared — the ledger then shows cash the bank does not have, and the bank rec will not balance until someone reverses the void. Checking the bank portal and placing a stop payment before voiding a mailed check is the order of operations.
scr_ap_void_a_check.ifSkipped: Stale and lost checks sit outstanding on the bank reconciliation indefinitely and eventually become an unclaimed property exposure.
gaap: State unclaimed property (escheat) statutes — dormancy periods for uncashed vendor checks
COSO 2013 — reversal controls with full audit trail
UCC §4-404 — bank not obliged to pay a check over six months old
redFlags: Voids dated into a closed, already-reported period
Checks voided without confirming they had not cleared
Stale checks voided to income instead of 2170 Unclaimed Property Payable
Void with no stop payment placed on a mailed check
scr_ap_void_a_check.yardi: Yardi Voyager: Payables > Check > Void Check, choosing the void date and period and whether to reverse the underlying payable.

scr_ap_generating_a_payment_file_2.purpose: Builds the ACH or electronic payment file from selected payment requests — one file per bank — for transmission to the bank in its required format, with a Confirm step once the bank has accepted and disbursed.
scr_ap_generating_a_payment_file_2.outcome: A correctly formatted NACHA or bank-proprietary file reaches the originating bank, and the confirmation closes the loop so the same payments are not generated again.
scr_ap_generating_a_payment_file_2.rootCause: An ACH file is effectively irrevocable once transmitted — NACHA gives the originator no unilateral right to pull an entry back, only a reversal request the receiver can refuse. Everything therefore has to be right before Generate: the effective date against the bank's cutoff, the prenote status of newly added vendor bank accounts, and the file totals against the payment proposal. Generating twice without confirming the first transmission is the classic way a property funds the same batch twice.
scr_ap_generating_a_payment_file_2.ifSkipped: Approved electronic payments never reach the bank, vendors go unpaid despite the system showing them paid, and terms are blown.
gaap: NACHA Operating Rules — ACH origination, prenotification and effective entry dates
COSO 2013 — dual control over funds transmission
SOC 1 — controls over files transmitted to financial institutions
OFAC sanctions screening of payees
redFlags: Files generated twice for the same payment requests with no confirmation between
Effective dates set past the bank's cutoff so funding lands a day late
New vendor bank accounts included before the prenote cleared
File totals not tied to the payment proposal before transmission
scr_ap_generating_a_payment_file_2.yardi: Yardi Voyager: Payables > EFT (ACH) file generation per bank, with origination settings from Setup > Bank.

scr_ap_open_close_the_a_p_period.purpose: Opens or closes the payables subledger for an entity or entity group and a chosen period, controlling whether invoices, payments and adjustments can still be booked into that month.
scr_ap_open_close_the_a_p_period.outcome: Once closed, no further payables activity can reach the period, so the 2010 Accounts Payable balance supporting the issued financials is frozen.
scr_ap_open_close_the_a_p_period.rootCause: The subledger close is what makes the owner's reported numbers durable. Leave A/P open and a late invoice posted a week after the statement shipped silently changes the expense and the payable the owner already read. The tension is real — invoices genuinely do arrive late — which is why the answer is an accrual booked before close, not an open period. Reopening must be a controller decision with a documented reason, because reopening means every downstream report has to be reissued.
scr_ap_open_close_the_a_p_period.ifSkipped: Backdated invoices land in a reported month, the owner's statement no longer agrees to the ledger, and the close has to be redone.

COSO 2013 — period-end close and cut-off controls

Entities closed on inconsistent dates within the same portfolio roll-up

scr_ap_a_p_single_scan.purpose: Enables direct scanner-to-invoice capture — the user turns on single scan upload in My preferences, installs the scanner connector, and then attaches the scanned image while creating the A/P invoice in one motion.
scr_ap_a_p_single_scan.outcome: Each invoice carries its source image from the moment of entry, so approvers and auditors see the document rather than taking the coding on trust.
scr_ap_a_p_single_scan.rootCause: An invoice without an attached image is an assertion. Approvers who cannot see the document approve the coding the entry clerk chose, which defeats the point of the approval. At year end the auditor's payables sample requests the supporting invoice for each selection, and images scanned later — or filed on a property shared drive — are the reason a sample turns into a scramble. Capturing at entry also fixes the invoice date and vendor against the document, which is what duplicate detection depends on.
scr_ap_a_p_single_scan.ifSkipped: Invoices are approved and paid without visible backup, and the audit sample cannot be supported without a manual document hunt.

scr_ap_approve_a_p_invoices.purpose: The approver's decision step for payables — open the Approval Workbench, filter to A/P Invoice, view the invoice and its backup, and approve, which releases the liability to post DR expense / CR 2010 Accounts Payable.
scr_ap_approve_a_p_invoices.outcome: Only invoices an authorized person has actually examined become liabilities and become eligible for payment.
scr_ap_approve_a_p_invoices.rootCause: Approval is the control the owner's management agreement is built on and the one an auditor tests first. Its weakness in practice is volume: an approver facing 300 invoices at month end clicks through them, and bulk approval without opening the backup makes the control exist on paper only. The self-approval prohibition matters just as much — an approver who entered the invoice has both custody and authorization, which is the segregation-of-duties failure that lets a fictitious vendor get paid.
scr_ap_approve_a_p_invoices.ifSkipped: Unexamined invoices post and pay, spending authority limits are meaningless, and the owner's control environment fails its SOC 1 test.
gaap: COSO 2013 — control environment, authorization, and segregation of duties
SOC 1 — approval evidence for the owner's service auditor
Management agreement delegation-of-authority limits
redFlags: Invoices approved by the person who entered them
Bulk approvals with no evidence the backup was opened

Invoices approved above the approver's documented limit

scr_ap_ai_finance_agent_roles_and_rights.purpose: Defines the permissions required to use the Finance Agent — the AI capture and coding assistant — determining who may let the agent read invoice images, propose GL codes and property allocations, and who must confirm them.
scr_ap_ai_finance_agent_roles_and_rights.outcome: AI-suggested coding is bounded by explicit rights, with a named human accountable for every code the agent proposes.
scr_ap_ai_finance_agent_roles_and_rights.rootCause: An AI that codes invoices is exercising judgment the owner delegated to a person, so the rights model has to make clear that the agent proposes and a human disposes. The specific hazard in multifamily is the capital-versus-expense call and the property allocation on a shared-services invoice: the agent pattern-matches to last month, which is exactly wrong when the scope changed. Granting agent rights to a user who can also approve collapses the maker-checker split into a single automated path to the GL.
scr_ap_ai_finance_agent_roles_and_rights.ifSkipped: AI-proposed coding posts unreviewed, and systematic miscoding propagates across every property the agent touches.

ASC 360-10-30 — capitalization judgments cannot be fully automated

AI-suggested codes accepted in bulk without sampling

scr_ap_approval_workbench_faqs.purpose: Collects the recurring approver questions — missing transactions, blocked approvals, what a disputed eInvoice means and how to clear one — as a single troubleshooting reference for approvers who are not accountants.
scr_ap_approval_workbench_faqs.outcome: Approvers resolve their own queue problems instead of letting invoices age while they wait for a support ticket.
scr_ap_approval_workbench_faqs.rootCause: Most approvers are property and regional managers, not accounting staff, and the moment their queue behaves unexpectedly they stop approving. That pause is the real cost: invoices sit past terms, the month-end accrual grows, and the A/P aging the owner sees shows a payables balance driven by workflow friction rather than by cash strategy. Documenting the common causes converts a support escalation into a two-minute self-fix.
scr_ap_approval_workbench_faqs.ifSkipped: Approvers abandon a queue they do not understand, invoices age past terms, and payables balloon for procedural rather than financial reasons.
gaap: COSO 2013 — information and communication supporting control operation
redFlags: Rising volume of aged pending approvals with no escalation
Approvers routinely raising tickets for issues answered in this reference

scr_ap_why_am_i_not_seeing_all_transacti.purpose: Diagnoses a queue that looks incomplete — confirming the page is Approval Workbench - My Approvals rather than the Spend Management Workbench, clearing saved views, clearing filters, and un-grouping columns that collapse rows out of sight.
scr_ap_why_am_i_not_seeing_all_transacti.outcome: The approver sees the complete population of items awaiting them, so nothing ages because it was hidden behind a view.
scr_ap_why_am_i_not_seeing_all_transacti.rootCause: A saved view is a persistent filter that survives logout, and an approver who saved one months ago has no reason to suspect it is still narrowing their queue. Column grouping is worse because the rows are present but collapsed, so the count looks plausible. The accounting consequence is a silent one: invoices that never appear are never chased, they simply become part of the received-not-invoiced accrual nobody can explain at close.
scr_ap_why_am_i_not_seeing_all_transacti.ifSkipped: Invoices hidden by a saved view or a collapsed grouping age indefinitely, and the close accrual absorbs a backlog nobody knew existed.
gaap: COSO 2013 — completeness of the population subject to a control
SOC 1 — control operated over the whole population, not a filtered subset
redFlags: Default saved views that exclude a transaction type or a property
Approvers whose queue count never changes

scr_ap_why_cant_i_approve_an_invoice.purpose: Explains the configuration blocks that stop an approval — a line coded to the default G/L account while Do Not Allow Posting to Default G/L is on, or a vendor that requires a purchase order on an invoice never matched to one, flagged by the information icon in the Actions column.
scr_ap_why_cant_i_approve_an_invoice.outcome: The approver understands the block is a deliberate control and routes the invoice for recoding or PO matching instead of escalating it as a defect.
scr_ap_why_cant_i_approve_an_invoice.rootCause: These blocks are the system refusing to let a control be bypassed. The default-G/L block exists because an invoice sitting in a suspense account distorts every operating statement it touches and is almost never cleaned up afterwards. The PO-required block exists because a vendor flagged that way is one the owner decided must go through commitment control — usually a contractor — and approving without the match defeats three-way matching entirely.
scr_ap_why_cant_i_approve_an_invoice.ifSkipped: Approvers treat a control as a bug, pressure support to disable it, and invoices post to suspense accounts or bypass PO matching.
gaap: COSO 2013 — preventive controls and three-way match

Management agreement purchasing policy
redFlags: Requests to disable the default G/L block instead of recoding
POs created after the invoice arrived purely to satisfy the match
Invoices sitting blocked for weeks with no recoding action

scr_ap_what_does_dispute_mean_on_an_einv.purpose: Defines the Dispute action, available only on electronic invoices, which sends the approver's comment and reason directly to the vendor over incorrect pricing, missing items or an owed credit — the comments go to the vendor verbatim.
scr_ap_what_does_dispute_mean_on_an_einv.outcome: A pricing or quantity disagreement is raised in writing to the vendor and recorded against the invoice rather than settled in an untracked email thread.
scr_ap_what_does_dispute_mean_on_an_einv.rootCause: Disputes that live in email never reach the ledger. The invoice either sits approved and gets paid at the wrong amount, or it sits unapproved and ages with no visible reason, and at close the accountant cannot tell whether to accrue the full amount or the contested one. Routing the dispute through the invoice creates the record that supports the accrual and, if the amount is material and the outcome uncertain, the ASC 450 assessment. That the comment reaches the vendor verbatim also means it is discoverable in a fee dispute.
scr_ap_what_does_dispute_mean_on_an_einv.ifSkipped: Pricing disagreements live in email, the invoice is paid at the disputed amount or ages unexplained, and the accrual has no support.
gaap: ASC 450-20 — loss contingencies for contested amounts
ASC 405-20 — a contested amount remains a liability until settled or released
COSO 2013 — documented resolution of exceptions
redFlags: Disputes raised with vague or intemperate comments that go straight to the vendor
Disputed invoices excluded from the month-end accrual
Disputes used to delay payment on invoices that are not actually contested

scr_ap_how_do_i_resolve_a_disputed_einvo.purpose: Closes out a dispute through the Resolve option that appears only on disputed invoices — entering a note explaining the resolution and choosing Clear Dispute alone, or Clear Dispute with the Approve check box to clear and approve in a single action.
scr_ap_how_do_i_resolve_a_disputed_einvo.outcome: The contested invoice returns to the normal approval path with a written record of how the disagreement was settled.
scr_ap_how_do_i_resolve_a_disputed_einvo.rootCause: Disputes get raised far more readily than they get closed, and an invoice stuck in dispute is invisible to the payment run while still sitting in the aging. At close the accountant needs to know whether the balance is real, reduced, or gone, and the resolution note is the only durable evidence of which. Combining Clear Dispute with Approve is efficient but skips a second look at whether the vendor actually issued the credit that was agreed, so the credit memo can be forgotten entirely.
scr_ap_how_do_i_resolve_a_disputed_einvo.ifSkipped: Invoices stay frozen in dispute, the aging shows amounts nobody is working, and agreed credits are never recorded.
gaap: ASC 450-20 — resolution of a contingency once the amount becomes determinable
ASC 705-20 — vendor consideration recognized when the credit is agreed
COSO 2013 — exception clearance with documented rationale
redFlags: Disputes cleared with no explanatory note
Disputes resolved by approving the original amount with no credit received
Long-dormant disputed invoices still counted at full value in the aging

scr_ap_about_the_approval_policy_manager.purpose: Introduces the Company application's Approval policy manager, where individual approval policies are created and then organized into workflows, gated by Approver permissions and by approvals being enabled for the transaction type on the Approval configuration page.
scr_ap_about_the_approval_policy_manager.outcome: The owner's delegation-of-authority matrix exists as configured policy rather than as a PDF nobody enforces.
scr_ap_about_the_approval_policy_manager.rootCause: Every management agreement contains spending limits, and in most portfolios those limits live in a document while the system approves on whatever was configured years ago. The policy manager is where the two are reconciled. Two prerequisites trip people up: without Approver permissions the policies cannot be built, and without approvals enabled for the transaction type the policies are built and then simply never fire, which gives the false comfort of a control that does not run.
scr_ap_about_the_approval_policy_manager.ifSkipped: Approval routing reflects an outdated matrix, or policies exist but never execute because the transaction type was never enabled.

SOC 1 — design of approval controls tested by the owner's service auditor
Management agreement authority limits
redFlags: Policies configured but the transaction type never enabled for approvals
Approval limits in the system that do not match the management agreement
Policy changes made without a documented change request

scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_by_user.purpose: Builds a policy routing every matching transaction to a named user or to a role, with a required count of one to four approvers when a role is chosen, and additional role or user rows added as needed.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_by_user.outcome: Routing is defined by position rather than by whoever happens to be available, and the required number of approvals is enforced by configuration.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_by_user.rootCause: Routing to a named individual is the most brittle configuration in the whole approval model: the person leaves, goes on holiday, or moves regions, and the queue stops dead with no alert. Routing to a role with a required count survives turnover and is what an auditor wants to see, because it demonstrates the control belongs to a position with defined authority rather than to a person. The required-approver count is also the mechanism that enforces dual approval on higher-risk categories.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_by_user.ifSkipped: Approvals route to individuals who leave or go absent, queues stall silently, and staff work around the block by re-entering transactions.
gaap: COSO 2013 — assignment of authority and responsibility to defined roles
SOC 1 — approval control continuity through personnel change
redFlags: Policies pointing at terminated users
Single-approver routing on high-value transaction types
No backup or delegate configured for a sole named approver

scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_based_o.purpose: Creates a threshold policy — an Amount from and Amount to band, a role or user responsible for it, and up to four required approval levels — so transactions inside that dollar range route to the person whose authority covers them.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_based_o.outcome: Spending authority limits from the management agreement are enforced automatically at the dollar level rather than by memory.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_based_o.rootCause: Amount bands are where a delegation-of-authority matrix becomes machinery, and the classic defect is a gap or overlap at the boundary: a band ending at $5,000 and the next starting at $5,001 is correct, while one starting at $5,000 double-routes and one starting at $5,002 leaves a dollar unrouted. Just as important is what the amount is measured against — an invoice total split across two lines or two invoices from the same vendor on the same day is the standard way a limit gets circumvented.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_based_o.ifSkipped: Transactions above delegated authority post with no senior review, and the owner's spending limits exist only on paper.
gaap: COSO 2013 — authorization limits as a preventive control activity
Management agreement delegation-of-authority thresholds
SOC 1 — threshold enforcement evidence
redFlags: Gaps or overlaps between amount bands
Invoices repeatedly split just below a threshold by the same vendor
Thresholds unchanged after the owner revised the management agreement

scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_tie.purpose: Configures escalating approval — successive rows each carrying a dollar range, a responsible role or user and a required approver level, with the final row's Amount to left blank so the top tier catches everything above it.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_tie.outcome: Larger transactions accumulate additional approvals as they climb the tiers, and no amount escapes because the top band is unbounded.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_tie.rootCause: Tiering is how an owner scales scrutiny to exposure: a $400 plumbing call and a $180,000 roof replacement should not receive the same review. The configuration detail that decides whether it works is the blank Amount to on the last row — leave a finite ceiling there and the highest-value transactions in the portfolio, the ones the owner most wants seen, fall outside every tier and route nowhere. Tiers also have to reflect whether approvals stack cumulatively or replace each other, which changes who is on the hook.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_tie.ifSkipped: Large capital and contract payments receive the same single approval as a routine supply invoice, or fall outside every tier entirely.
gaap: COSO 2013 — risk-proportionate control activities
Management agreement escalation thresholds
ASC 360-10-30 — capital spend warranting elevated review
redFlags: Final tier with a finite Amount to, leaving the largest transactions unrouted
Tier boundaries that do not match the owner's escalation matrix
Tiers configured so a single person satisfies two consecutive levels

scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_s.purpose: Routes transactions by payee — selecting a Vendor from and Vendor to range in the alphabetical vendor list, with a responsible role or user and required approver level for that range.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_s.outcome: Transactions for sensitive or high-risk payees are seen by a specific reviewer regardless of the dollar amount involved.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_s.rootCause: Some payees warrant review whatever the amount: an affiliate of the owner, the property management company itself, an attorney handling a litigated eviction, or a contractor on a watch list after a quality dispute. Amount-based policies miss all of these because the invoices are often small. Affiliate payees are the sharpest case — under ASC 850 these are related-party transactions the owner must disclose, and routing them to a designated reviewer is how they are identified rather than reconstructed from the vendor master in December.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_s.ifSkipped: Related-party and watch-list vendors are paid through routine approval, and related-party disclosure is rebuilt from scratch at year end.
gaap: ASC 850-10-50 — related-party transaction identification and disclosure
COSO 2013 — targeted controls over higher-risk counterparties
Management agreement affiliate transaction approval requirements
redFlags: Alphabetical vendor ranges that break when a new vendor is added inside the range
Affiliate vendors with no dedicated approval policy
Vendor-range policies never reviewed after vendor master cleanups

scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_v.purpose: Routes by vendor classification rather than by individual payee — selecting a Vendor type and the role or user responsible for approving everything carrying that classification, with the required approver level.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_v.outcome: Whole categories of spend — construction trades, professional services, utilities — route to the reviewer who understands them, and new vendors inherit the routing automatically.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_v.rootCause: Vendor type is the only routing dimension that survives vendor master growth: add a new HVAC contractor and it inherits the trade's approval path without anyone touching the policy. That strength is also the weakness, because the whole thing depends on the type being set correctly at vendor setup, and a contractor miscoded as a general supplier bypasses the construction reviewer along with the lien-waiver and certificate-of-insurance checks that reviewer performs. Vendor type usually also drives the 1099 default, so the error compounds at year end.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_v.ifSkipped: New vendors route to generic approvers, and trade-specific checks such as lien waivers and insurance verification are never applied.

State mechanic's lien statutes — lien waiver collection from construction trades
IRC §6041 — vendor classification driving 1099 treatment
redFlags: Contractors classified as general suppliers, bypassing lien-waiver checks
Vendor types added to the master with no matching approval policy
Type-based routing overlapping a vendor-specific policy with unclear precedence

scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_g.purpose: Routes on coding — a G/L account from and to range, or a defined G/L account group, sent to the role or user responsible for that range, so accounts such as travel and entertainment or capital additions always reach a specific reviewer.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_g.outcome: Sensitive account lines are reviewed by someone who understands what belongs in them, independent of vendor or amount.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_g.rootCause: Account-based routing is the only control that catches the capital-versus-expense decision at the point it is made. Anything coded to 1530 Building Improvements or 1410 Construction in Progress changes the balance sheet, the depreciation schedule and the owner's NOI, and it deserves a reviewer who will ask whether the work extended the asset's life or merely maintained it. The same logic covers discretionary accounts under 6410 Administrative, where owners want visibility regardless of size. The gap to watch is what happens when an invoice spans several accounts across different policies.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_g.ifSkipped: Capital items are expensed and discretionary spend goes unseen, distorting both NOI and the depreciable basis reported to the owner.

COSO 2013 — account-level review controls
ASC 250-10 — prevention rather than correction of classification errors
redFlags: Multi-line invoices spanning policies with ambiguous routing
Capital accounts excluded from the account-based policy range
Account ranges not updated after a chart of accounts change

scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_j.purpose: Routes every transaction charged to a specific job — a named renovation, a roof replacement, a unit turn program — to the person accountable for that job's budget, independent of vendor or amount.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_j.outcome: The project owner sees every cost hitting their job before it posts, so the job's committed and actual costs stay under one person's control.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_j.rootCause: Job cost overruns are discovered at the wrong time — when the draw package is assembled and the total does not match the budget. Routing by job puts the construction manager in front of each invoice while there is still room to challenge it, and it also puts the person who knows whether the work was actually performed in the approval path. On lender-funded projects this matters twice over, because costs charged to a job that the lender's budget does not recognize are costs the owner funds from equity.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_j.ifSkipped: Costs land on a job without the project owner's knowledge, and the overrun surfaces only when the draw fails to reconcile.

Construction loan agreement draw and budget line requirements

scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_j.purpose: Routes by job classification rather than by individual job — capital projects, unit turns, insurance restoration, tenant improvements — so every job of that kind inherits the same approval path as it is created.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_j.outcome: New jobs of a given class route correctly from the day they open, without anyone remembering to build a policy for each one.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_j.rootCause: A portfolio opens jobs continuously — every unit turn, every storm repair — and per-job policies cannot keep pace, so jobs open with no routing and their costs approve through the generic path. Classifying by type fixes that, and it also lets the owner apply genuinely different scrutiny where the accounting differs: insurance restoration jobs carry recovery receivables and deductible splits, capital jobs feed the depreciation schedule, and turn jobs are usually expensed. One approval path for all three guarantees at least two of them are reviewed by the wrong person.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_j.ifSkipped: Newly opened jobs carry no routing, their costs approve generically, and insurance or capital jobs are reviewed as if they were routine turns.
gaap: ASC 360-10-30 — capitalization by project class
ASC 610-30 — insurance recoveries on involuntary conversions
COSO 2013 — standardized routing across a class of transactions

scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_c.purpose: Routes at the cost-code level inside a job — concrete, roofing, electrical, general conditions — sending transactions coded to a given code to the role or user who owns that trade line.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_c.outcome: Trade-level costs are reviewed by the person who knows that trade's contract, schedule of values and retainage terms.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_c.rootCause: Cost-code routing is what makes a schedule of values enforceable. The person approving a roofing invoice needs to know the roofing contract value, what percentage is complete, and what retainage has been withheld — knowledge a generic approver does not have. It is also the level at which cost shifting is caught: charges moved from an overspent code into general conditions look fine at the job total and hide the fact that one trade is running well over. Retainage withheld at the wrong code misstates 2015 Retainage Payable by trade.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_c.ifSkipped: Costs migrate between trade lines to mask overruns, and retainage is withheld at the wrong code, misstating what is owed to each subcontractor.

scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_an_.purpose: Inserts an accounting review step into the A/P invoice path, routing every invoice to a designated accounting reviewer in addition to the operational approvers who authorize the spend.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_an_.outcome: Somebody with accounting competence checks period, property and GL coding after the operational approver has confirmed the spend was legitimate.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_an_.rootCause: Operational and accounting approval answer different questions. A property manager confirms the work happened and the price is fair; they are not evaluating whether the service period falls before the cut-off, whether the cost belongs to this entity, or whether the coding is capital. Without a dedicated accounting reviewer those judgments are made by the entry clerk and never checked, and they surface as reclassification entries after the owner statement has already gone out. This step is also the offshore-onshore review handoff in most delivery models.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_an_.ifSkipped: Coding and cut-off errors reach the ledger unchecked and are found only during variance review, after the owner package has shipped.

ASC 250-10 — prevention of classification and period errors
