scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_j.purpose: Routes journal entries by their journal type — accrual, reclassification, allocation, intercompany, adjusting — to the role or user authorized to approve that class of entry.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_j.outcome: Manual journal entries are reviewed by someone qualified for the specific kind of adjustment, closing the largest unmonitored path into the general ledger.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_j.rootCause: Manual journal entries are the highest-risk postings in any ledger because they bypass every subledger control that surrounds invoices and receipts. Journal-type routing is how the risk is graded: a recurring monthly accrual reversal needs light review, while an intercompany entry moving balances between 1230 Due From Affiliates and 2130 Due To Affiliates is a related-party movement that needs a controller. Auditors consistently test manual entries for management override, and the journal-type policy is the design evidence that such entries were independently approved.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_j.ifSkipped: Self-approved manual entries reach the ledger, and the audit's management-override testing finds the control absent by design.
gaap: AU-C 240 / COSO 2013 — controls addressing management override through journal entries
ASC 850 — related-party and intercompany entries
ASC 250-10 — error correction entries
redFlags: Journal types with no approval policy attached
Preparers approving their own entries
Round-dollar or period-end entries clustered under a lightly-reviewed journal type
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_j.yardi: Yardi Voyager: journal entry workflow via Administration > Workflow with approvers set on the JE batch by journal type.

scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_p.purpose: Routes A/P payments by how the money moves — check, ACH, wire, virtual card — so each method carries the approval level its irrevocability and fraud profile warrant.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_p.outcome: Wires and ACH batches get the heavier scrutiny their finality demands, while routine check runs follow the standard path.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_p.rootCause: Payment methods are not equally recoverable. A wire is final on release; an ACH entry cannot be unilaterally recalled under NACHA rules once transmitted; a check can be stopped at the bank before presentation. Applying one approval standard to all three means either wires are under-controlled or check runs are strangled by unnecessary approvals. Method-based routing is also the practical defense against business email compromise, since the fraudster's preferred instruction is always a same-day wire.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_p.ifSkipped: Irrevocable wires and ACH files are released on the same authority as a routine check, and a fraudulent instruction succeeds on the first attempt.
gaap: NACHA Operating Rules — ACH origination authorization and irrevocability
UCC Article 4A — commercially reasonable security procedures for funds transfers
COSO 2013 — dual control over irrevocable disbursements
SOC 1 — payment release controls
redFlags: Wires approved at the same level as checks
Same-day wire requests originating from email instructions
Payment methods added without a corresponding approval policy

scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_b.purpose: Routes transactions by the bank account they draw on, so the account's signatories and the people approving disbursements from it are the same set the bank resolution names.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_b.outcome: Each bank account's disbursements route to the people actually authorized on that account, including restricted and trust accounts.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_b.rootCause: Property portfolios run accounts that are legally distinct: an operating account, a security deposit trust account, replacement reserve and tax escrow accounts controlled by the lender. The deposit trust account holds resident money the property does not own, and in most states disbursing from it for operating expenses is a statutory violation rather than a policy breach. Bank-account routing is the configuration that puts a different, senior approver in front of any movement from a restricted account, and it is also how system approvers are kept aligned with the bank's signature card.
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_b.ifSkipped: Restricted trust and escrow funds are disbursed on routine operating authority, creating a statutory violation and a lender covenant breach.
gaap: State security deposit trust statutes — segregation and permitted use of resident funds
COSO 2013 — controls over restricted assets
Loan agreement escrow and reserve disbursement covenants
ASC 210 — classification of restricted cash
redFlags: Deposit trust account disbursements routed through the operating approval path
System approvers not matching the bank signature card
Reserve draws approved without the lender's required documentation
scr_ap_adding_an_approval_policy_for_a_b.yardi: Yardi Voyager: bank-level controls from Setup > Bank combined with Administration > Workflow approvals scoped per bank account.

scr_ap_adding_approval_workflows_2.purpose: Assembles individual policies into a workflow — naming it, selecting the transaction types it governs, adding policies in sequence, scoping it to properties, and optionally enabling conditions that decide whether the workflow applies.
scr_ap_adding_approval_workflows_2.outcome: A complete routing chain exists per transaction type and property, so every submission finds a defined path from submitter to final approver.
scr_ap_adding_approval_workflows_2.rootCause: Policies in isolation do nothing; the workflow is what orders them and binds them to properties. Two configuration mistakes dominate. The first is property scope — a newly acquired asset added to the portfolio but not to any workflow, so its invoices approve on a default path or not at all. The second is policy sequence, where an amount tier sits ahead of the accounting reviewer and the reviewer ends up rubber-stamping something already authorized. Conditional logic makes both harder to see, which is why the configuration needs to be tested with a live transaction, not just saved.
scr_ap_adding_approval_workflows_2.ifSkipped: Newly acquired properties or new transaction types have no routing, and their transactions either stall or approve through an unintended default.
gaap: COSO 2013 — control activities deployed through policies and procedures across the entity
SOC 1 — completeness of control coverage across all in-scope properties
Management agreement authority structure
redFlags: Properties in the portfolio not covered by any workflow
Policy sequence placing accounting review after final authorization
Conditional logic that silently disables a workflow for a subset of transactions
Workflows saved but never tested with a live transaction

scr_ap_approving_and_declining_transacti.purpose: The Company-menu route into the Approval workbench — filter by transaction type, toggle between My approvals and View all, open a transaction with Edit or View, and approve or decline singly or in bulk by check box.
scr_ap_approving_and_declining_transacti.outcome: Approvers act on their queue from the Company application with the same decision record as the module-level path.
scr_ap_approving_and_declining_transacti.rootCause: The same workbench is reachable from several places, and users who arrive through Company often land on View all, where they can see every pending transaction across the portfolio but cannot act on the ones that are not theirs. The confusion produces two distinct failures: an approver who believes their queue is empty because they are looking at the wrong view, and a bulk approval made from a list broad enough that items outside the approver's actual authority get swept in. Decline needs a reason too, or the submitter gets a rejected invoice with no idea what to fix.
scr_ap_approving_and_declining_transacti.ifSkipped: Approvers misread which view they are in, queues sit untouched, and declines return to submitters with no actionable reason.
gaap: COSO 2013 — authorization performed by a person with the requisite authority
SOC 1 — approval evidence retained per transaction
redFlags: Bulk approvals covering more transactions than the approver could have reviewed
Declines recorded with no comment
Approvers working from View all rather than My approvals

scr_ap_accounts_payable_home_page.purpose: The payables landing page, grouping every entry point into Search & Find, Periodic Tasks and Reports — vendors, A/P invoices, posted payments, the invoice creation submenu, the document dashboard, vendor approval and the pay submenu covering payments, adjustments and advances.
scr_ap_accounts_payable_home_page.outcome: The daily payables cycle is reachable from one place, and the counts on the page show where the backlog actually is.
scr_ap_accounts_payable_home_page.rootCause: The home page is where an A/P clerk decides what to work on, and the risk is treating it as navigation rather than as a status board. Unapproved invoices, unposted payments and pending vendor approvals all surface here, and an aging pending-vendor-approval count is the specific tell that invoices are being held because a payee was never activated. Counts shown here are also filter-dependent, so a figure taken from the home page and quoted into a close status call can be wrong about the entity or period it covers.
scr_ap_accounts_payable_home_page.ifSkipped: Backlogs in vendor approval and unposted payments stay invisible until they surface as aged payables or a missed check run.
gaap: COSO 2013 — ongoing monitoring activities
ASC 450-20 — visibility of obligations requiring accrual at period end
redFlags: Growing pending vendor approval count blocking invoice entry
Home page counts quoted on close calls without confirming the entity and period filters
Unposted payments left in draft across a period end
scr_ap_accounts_payable_home_page.yardi: Yardi Voyager: the Payables module home and role-based dashboard widgets showing pending payables and approvals.

scr_ap_about_the_approval_workbench.purpose: Introduces the workbench as the single place pending transactions across modules are worked — a filters section controlling which transactions appear and a transaction list offering approve, close, decline, view, edit, add approver and export to Excel.
scr_ap_about_the_approval_workbench.outcome: Approvers have one queue spanning invoices, journal entries, payments and purchase orders instead of hunting through each module.
scr_ap_about_the_approval_workbench.rootCause: Before a consolidated workbench, approvals lived inside each module and items were missed simply because nobody looked in that module that week. Centralizing them makes the pending population visible and, critically, measurable — the aging of the pending queue becomes a reportable control metric the controller can monitor. The filter section is the hazard: it governs the population an approver believes is complete, so a filter left narrow makes an approver certain they are up to date while items age behind it.
scr_ap_about_the_approval_workbench.ifSkipped: Pending items scatter across modules, no one can state the total awaiting approval, and the accrual at close is built on guesswork.
gaap: COSO 2013 — monitoring activities and completeness of the control population
SOC 1 — centralized evidence of approval control operation
redFlags: Persistent filters narrowing the queue without the approver realizing
No monitoring of how long items sit pending
Transaction types enabled for approval but absent from the workbench
scr_ap_about_the_approval_workbench.yardi: Yardi Voyager: the 'My Approvals' inbox plus module-level Find screens for workflow-pending transactions.

scr_ap_filtering_transactions_in_the_app.purpose: Sets the workbench population — transaction type first, then type-specific criteria, with an Include declined option that surfaces declined items for edit and resubmission; selections persist across transaction types until Clear is clicked, and can be saved as a default view.
scr_ap_filtering_transactions_in_the_app.outcome: The approver works a deliberately scoped list and knows what the scope excluded, including declined items that would otherwise be invisible.
scr_ap_filtering_transactions_in_the_app.rootCause: Two behaviors on this screen cause real accounting damage. Filters persist when the transaction type changes, so criteria set for invoices silently carry into the journal entry queue and hide entries. And declined transactions are excluded by default, which means a declined invoice is out of everyone's sight — the approver's queue and the submitter's attention — until someone thinks to include declined. Those invoices are still liabilities that need accruing at close, and they are exactly the population that ages without explanation.
scr_ap_filtering_transactions_in_the_app.ifSkipped: Declined and filtered-out transactions vanish from view, age unworked, and turn up as unexplained items during the close accrual review.
gaap: COSO 2013 — completeness of the population subject to review
ASC 450-20 — accrual of obligations regardless of workflow status
SOC 1 — control applied to the full in-scope population
redFlags: Filters persisting across transaction types and hiding items
Declined invoices never revisited because the default view excludes them
Saved default views narrower than the approver's actual responsibility

scr_ap_approving_and_declining_transacti.purpose: The workbench's decision mechanics, which require the My Approvals view rather than View All — switching views with the My Approvals button, acting individually or in bulk, and using Review and approve to work A/P invoices back-to-back.
scr_ap_approving_and_declining_transacti.outcome: Decisions are recorded against the approver who actually holds the authority, with a view distinction that makes it clear when they do not.
scr_ap_approving_and_declining_transacti.rootCause: The View All and My Approvals split is the workbench's most consequential design detail: View All shows the whole portfolio's pending population for oversight, but action is only possible where authority exists. Approvers who do not understand the distinction conclude the system is broken and ask for broader rights, which is how approval authority quietly widens beyond the management agreement. The Review and approve back-to-back mode is efficient and dangerous in the same breath, because its rhythm encourages speed over examining each invoice's backup.
scr_ap_approving_and_declining_transacti.ifSkipped: Approvers cannot act, request rights beyond their authority, or move so fast through back-to-back review that the control stops functioning.
gaap: COSO 2013 — authorization by a person with appropriate authority and segregation of duties
SOC 1 — approver identity and decision evidence
Management agreement delegation-of-authority limits
redFlags: Approval rights widened because users found View All confusing
Review and approve sessions clearing dozens of invoices in minutes
Approvals recorded against a user who was not the reviewer

scr_ap_exporting_transactions_to_excel.purpose: Exports the workbench's current transaction list to Excel, carrying exactly the columns enabled in the workbench, from either the Approval workbench or the Spend management workbench.
scr_ap_exporting_transactions_to_excel.outcome: A point-in-time list of pending items exists outside the system for a close call, an owner question or an audit evidence package.
scr_ap_exporting_transactions_to_excel.rootCause: The export inherits the columns and the filters showing at that moment, which makes it a snapshot of a view rather than of the pending population. Two things follow. An export used to support the received-not-invoiced accrual understates the liability if the view excluded declined or filtered items, and the number handed to the owner is wrong by a full accrual cycle. And the file carries vendor names, amounts and property detail out of the platform onto a laptop or a shared drive, which moves it outside the SOC 1 boundary the owner's auditor relies on.
scr_ap_exporting_transactions_to_excel.ifSkipped: Pending approvals cannot be evidenced at a point in time, and the close accrual and audit package rest on a screen nobody can reproduce.
gaap: SOC 1 — data leaving the service organization's control boundary
COSO 2013 — completeness and accuracy of information produced by the entity
ASC 450-20 — support for accrued obligations at period end
redFlags: Exports used as accrual support without the filter criteria documented alongside
Stale exports circulated after a later invoice batch posted
Vendor-level exports stored on unsecured personal drives
Column set omitting amount or property, making the export unusable as evidence

scr_ap_adding_an_approver_to_a_transacti.purpose: Lets an approver pull another user into a specific transaction through the Add approver link — recording a comment explaining why and selecting from users who already have access to that transaction's location.
scr_ap_adding_an_approver_to_a_transacti.outcome: A second opinion is obtained on one transaction with the request and its reason written into the approval history.
scr_ap_adding_an_approver_to_a_transacti.rootCause: Ad hoc approvers are how genuine judgment gets into the chain — an approver who cannot tell whether the scope on a restoration invoice was actually performed pulls in the maintenance supervisor who was on site. But an added approver is an approval path the configured workflow did not design, so it must be additive, never a substitute for a required level. The location constraint is the real safeguard here: it stops someone routing a transaction to a friendly colleague with no responsibility for that property.
scr_ap_adding_an_approver_to_a_transacti.ifSkipped: Approvers guess at transactions they cannot evaluate, or route them informally by email with no record of who was consulted.
gaap: COSO 2013 — authorization supplemented, not replaced, by ad hoc review
SOC 1 — the approval chain as evidenced must match the designed control
redFlags: Added approvers replacing rather than supplementing a required level
Same pair of users repeatedly adding each other
Approvers added with no comment explaining why

scr_ap_sending_a_transaction_back_to_the.purpose: Returns a multi-level transaction to the approver who already signed it, with a required comment, singly or in bulk by check box — the item leaves the current approver's queue and reappears in the prior approver's.
scr_ap_sending_a_transaction_back_to_the.outcome: A question about an earlier approval goes back to the person who made it, preserving the workflow instead of restarting it with a decline.
scr_ap_sending_a_transaction_back_to_the.rootCause: Declining a multi-level transaction sends it all the way back to the submitter and destroys the approvals already given, so the whole chain has to be rebuilt for what may be a single clarification. Send back is the proportionate action, and the comment is what makes it useful — the previous approver needs to know what to reconsider. The exposure is the handoff itself: the item leaves the current queue immediately, so if the prior approver is absent it can sit in a queue no one is monitoring while the invoice ages toward its due date.
scr_ap_sending_a_transaction_back_to_the.ifSkipped: Minor clarifications become full declines, approval chains restart from the submitter, and invoices miss their payment terms over a question.
gaap: COSO 2013 — exception handling with documented rationale within the control
SOC 1 — complete approval history including returns
redFlags: Transactions bounced repeatedly between the same two approvers
Send back used to an absent approver with no delegate
Bulk send back applied without a transaction-specific reason

scr_ap_viewing_an_attachment_for_a_trans.purpose: Opens the document attached to a transaction directly from the approval queue via the Actions column icon, so the approver reads the vendor's invoice, contract or lien waiver before deciding.
scr_ap_viewing_an_attachment_for_a_trans.outcome: The approval decision is made against the source document rather than against the coding someone else typed.
scr_ap_viewing_an_attachment_for_a_trans.rootCause: An approval given without opening the attachment is an approval of the data-entry clerk's judgment, which is the opposite of what the control is for. The document is where the duplicate becomes obvious, where the service period that straddles the cut-off appears, and where a contractor invoice reveals whether the lien waiver is attached. It is also the evidence the auditor requests: SOC 1 sampling asks for the invoice behind the approval, and an approval with no retrievable document is a control exception no matter who clicked it.
scr_ap_viewing_an_attachment_for_a_trans.ifSkipped: Approvals rest on typed coding alone, duplicates and wrong service periods pass, and the audit sample has no supporting document.
gaap: SOC 1 — documentary evidence supporting approval controls
COSO 2013 — approval supported by relevant, verifiable information
State mechanic's lien statutes — lien waiver review before payment to a contractor
redFlags: Approvals recorded on transactions with no attachment
Attachment that is a statement or quote rather than the invoice
Contractor invoices approved without the conditional lien waiver attached
scr_ap_viewing_an_attachment_for_a_trans.yardi: Yardi Voyager: Document Management (DMS) attachments opened from the payable in the PAYscan approval queue.

scr_ap_viewing_the_available_budget_for_.purpose: Opens the Available budget page from the dollar-sign link in the Actions column, showing the budget for the property and account on the transaction so the approver sees remaining budget before committing the spend.
scr_ap_viewing_the_available_budget_for_.outcome: Approval becomes a budget decision, with the overage visible at the moment of authorization rather than at month-end variance review.
scr_ap_viewing_the_available_budget_for_.rootCause: Budget variance explanations written three weeks after the fact are archaeology; the only time the spend can actually be questioned is before it is approved. Putting available budget in front of the approver is what turns the budget from a reporting artifact into a control. The figure has to be trusted though — it must come from the owner-approved published budget version, and whether it nets outstanding purchase-order commitments decides whether remaining budget is real or already spent. An approver reading an uncommitted figure will authorize spend that is not there.
scr_ap_viewing_the_available_budget_for_.ifSkipped: Approvers authorize spend with no idea of remaining budget, and overruns are discovered only when the owner reads the variance report.
gaap: COSO 2013 — budgetary control as a preventive control activity
Management agreement budget authority and overage approval thresholds
redFlags: Available budget shown from a draft rather than the owner-approved published version
Remaining budget not net of open purchase-order commitments
Repeated approvals against lines already fully consumed
scr_ap_viewing_the_available_budget_for_.yardi: Yardi Voyager: budget-versus-actual checks in the PAYscan/Procure to Pay approval screen against the posted Voyager budget.

scr_ap_viewing_the_approval_history_of_a.purpose: Opens the approval history for a transaction through the Status column link — after filtering the workbench and optionally switching to View all — showing each approver, action, timestamp and comment in sequence.
scr_ap_viewing_the_approval_history_of_a.outcome: The full chain of who did what and when is retrievable per transaction and can be exported as audit evidence.
scr_ap_viewing_the_approval_history_of_a.rootCause: Approval history is the evidence the control existed, and it is the first artifact requested when anything goes wrong — a disputed payment, a suspected override, or a SOC 1 sample. What it exposes is often more interesting than the fact of approval: a transaction approved sixty seconds after submission by someone who could not have read it, an approver added and then removed, or a send-back loop that shows a disagreement nobody documented. Filing the exported trail with the month-end work papers is what makes it usable months later when the people involved have moved on.
scr_ap_viewing_the_approval_history_of_a.ifSkipped: There is no retrievable proof of who authorized a payment, and the SOC 1 control is untestable for that transaction.
gaap: SOC 1 — evidence that the approval control operated for the sampled transaction
COSO 2013 — monitoring and accountability through audit trails
AU-C 240 — evidence relevant to management override
redFlags: Approvals timestamped seconds after submission on high-value invoices
Approvers added then removed with no comment
History showing a single user completing consecutive approval levels
scr_ap_viewing_the_approval_history_of_a.yardi: Yardi Voyager: workflow history on the payable record plus Administration > User Activity / Change Log reports.

scr_ap_adding_an_approver_during_the_rev.purpose: Adds an approver without leaving the back-to-back Review and Approve flow — the A/P invoice page exposes Add approver and Approval comments fields, and the reviewer continues with Approve & next.
scr_ap_adding_an_approver_during_the_rev.outcome: A questionable invoice picks up an extra reviewer mid-session without breaking the reviewer's rhythm through the rest of the queue.
scr_ap_adding_an_approver_during_the_rev.rootCause: Back-to-back review exists to clear volume, and the moment an invoice raises a question the reviewer faces a bad choice: stop and lose the session, decline something that is probably fine, or approve it and hope. Adding an approver in-flight is the escape valve that keeps the control honest under volume pressure. The comment field is the part that matters, because an approver appearing on an invoice with no stated reason tells a later reader nothing, and the invoice now depends on a person who may not know they were added.
scr_ap_adding_an_approver_during_the_rev.ifSkipped: Reviewers under queue pressure approve invoices they have doubts about rather than interrupt the session to escalate.
gaap: COSO 2013 — escalation as part of control activity design
SOC 1 — approval chain evidence including in-flight additions
redFlags: Approvers added with a blank Approval comments field
Added approvers never notified, leaving the invoice stalled
In-flight additions concentrated on a single vendor

scr_ap_reviewing_approved_invoices.purpose: Runs the Approval History Audit report over a date range filtered to Accounts Payable Invoices, showing every transaction that went through or is still in the approval cycle, with location filtering used to examine how a single user has been approving.
scr_ap_reviewing_approved_invoices.outcome: A period-level view of approval behavior that evidences the control for the auditor and exposes approvers whose pattern does not look like review.
scr_ap_reviewing_approved_invoices.rootCause: Per-transaction history proves one approval happened; this report is what shows whether the control is actually working across a population. Patterns only appear in aggregate — one approver clearing a month of invoices in a single sitting, approvals consistently just under a threshold, or a property where the same person submits and approves. This is the report the owner's SOC 1 auditor asks for to select their sample, and it is the report the controller should be running before the auditor does, so the exceptions are explained rather than discovered.
scr_ap_reviewing_approved_invoices.ifSkipped: Approval behavior is never examined in aggregate, and the auditor discovers the rubber-stamping pattern before management does.
gaap: SOC 1 — population report supporting the service auditor's sample selection
COSO 2013 — monitoring activities evaluating whether controls operate as designed
AU-C 240 — analysis of approval patterns for override indicators
Management agreement authority limits
redFlags: Approvers clearing hundreds of invoices in a single short session
Approvals clustered immediately below an authority threshold
Same user appearing as submitter and approver at a property
Report never run between audit cycles
scr_ap_reviewing_approved_invoices.yardi: Yardi Voyager: workflow audit reporting from Administration > User Activity / Change Log combined with PAYscan approval history extracts.
